title: Which tree do you see the most on your way to school?
description: A question from the book asks you to record the trees you see on a walk and fill a table. The video runs the plan of tallying, tabulating and comparing, and reads the three questions from the table.
teaching_notes: One idea: record while you walk, fill the table, then read the largest, the smallest and any tie from it. Watch for children who count a tree twice or who forget that two trees can have the same count.

source: Figure it Out: record the trees seen on the way from home to school and fill in the table
video_script.why: The child collects their own data and reads the largest, the smallest and any tie from a table.
video_script.substitution: none: the question asks for the child's own observation, so no numbers are fixed
video_script.anchor: the trees on your way from home to school
video_script.payoff_line: The answers depend on the trees you see on your own way.

final_answer.spoken: the answers depend on the trees you see on your own way

hold_back: depend on the trees you see
maths_rules: No count is fixed: the answer depends on the child's own walk.
If two trees have the same count, they share the place in the comparison.
video_script.design: A road from a house to a school with trees along it, and an empty two-column table of tree names and counts.

beats.on_screen: title card with a road from a house to a school, and different trees along the road

marks.scene: the title card arrives with the road and the trees

marks.ask: a question mark lights up above the trees

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about the trees on your way to school.
<bookmark mark='walk'/>Some trees stand in large numbers, and some stand in small numbers.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Which tree do you see the most?

beats.on_screen: the road, the trees and the question mark stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: the road with trees and an empty table with two columns, Tree and No. of trees, with rows Peepal and Neem

beats.on_screen: Given: the trees you see on the way from home to school
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the trees that you see on your way from home to school.

beats.on_screen: To find: a. the tree seen the most, b. the tree seen the least, c. whether two trees have the same count

marks.find: the three lines to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the largest count, the smallest count, and any tie.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: name a few trees and make one tally row for each

marks.names: tree names are written down the first column
marks.tally: a tally mark is drawn for each tree seen while walking

narration: <bookmark mark='names'/>Step one, write the names of a few trees in the table.
<bookmark mark='tally'/>As you walk, draw one tally mark for each tree that you see.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: read each row of tally marks and write its count in the table

marks.count: each row of tally marks is read as bundles of five and loose strokes, and its count is written

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step two, read each row of tally marks and write its count.
Count a bundle as five, then add the loose strokes.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: compare the counts: circle the largest and underline the smallest
narration: <bookmark mark='compare'/>Step three, compare the counts in the table.
The largest count belongs to the tree seen the most.
<bookmark mark='least'/>The smallest count belongs to the tree seen the least.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: look for two rows with the same count

marks.tie: two rows with equal counts are joined by a bracket

narration: <bookmark mark='tie'/>Step four, look for two trees with the same count.
If you find them, the answer to the last question is yes.

beats.on_screen: Answer: it depends on your own observation; the table tells the largest, the smallest and any tie
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The answers depend on the trees you see on your own way.
Your table will tell the most, the least and any tie.
